prompt: A small business needs Windows 11 workstations that can join an Active Directory domain and use BitLocker encryption. What is the MINIMUM required edition?

options.text: Windows 11 Home
Windows 11 Pro
Windows 11 S Mode
Windows 11 IoT

explanation: Windows 11 Pro includes: Active Directory domain join, BitLocker full-disk encryption, Group Policy editor (gpedit.msc), Hyper-V, Remote Desktop host, Windows Sandbox. Windows 11 Home lacks ALL enterprise features — no domain join, no BitLocker, no Group Policy. Windows 11 Enterprise adds AppLocker, advanced Defender features, BranchCache — requires volume licensing. Windows 11 Education: similar to Enterprise for academic institutions. S Mode: restricted to Microsoft Store apps only. For any exam question involving domain join OR BitLocker, the answer is Pro or higher. Pro for Workstations adds NVMe/RAID optimizations and higher RAM limits.

prompt: Which ipconfig flag displays the full IP configuration including MAC address, DHCP server address, and lease expiration time?

options.text: ipconfig /release
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /flushdns
ipconfig /renew

explanation: ipconfig /all: full network details — IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, Physical Address (MAC), DHCP enabled status, DHCP server IP, lease obtained/expires. ipconfig (no flag): shows IP, mask, gateway only — no MAC, no DHCP details. ipconfig /release: releases current DHCP lease (IP goes away). ipconfig /renew: requests a new DHCP lease. ipconfig /flushdns: clears the local DNS resolver cache — fixes stale DNS entries causing wrong-site redirects. ipconfig /registerdns: re-registers the computer's hostname with DNS. For troubleshooting, /all gives the most diagnostic information in a single command.

prompt: User Alice is in Group A (Read) and Group B (Modify) for a folder. Group C has Deny Write for the same folder, and Alice is also in Group C. What are Alice's effective permissions?

options.text: Modify — most permissive wins
Read only — Deny Write blocks the Write part of Modify
Full Control — multiple groups grant everything
No Access — any Deny overrides all permissions

explanation: NTFS effective permissions = UNION of all Allow permissions MINUS any explicit Deny. Alice gets: Read (from Group A) + Modify (from Group B) — combined = Modify. But Deny Write (from Group C) removes the Write component of Modify. Result: Alice can read and execute but cannot write or delete. Deny removes a specific right, not all access. Only an explicit Deny Full Control or Deny Read would block all access. Key rules: 1. Allow permissions from multiple groups are combined (most permissive). 2. Explicit Deny overrides Allow for that specific permission. 3. Deny Full Control = no access regardless of other groups.

prompt: A technician needs to edit a setting that affects only the currently logged-in user's environment, not other users on the same machine. Which registry hive should be modified?

options.text: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM)
HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU)
HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR)
HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC)

explanation: HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU): stores settings for the currently logged-in user — desktop wallpaper, user-specific app settings, printer preferences, personal environment variables. Changes here only affect the current user's profile. HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM): machine-wide settings affecting ALL users — hardware, installed software, system-wide policies. HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR): file extension associations and COM registration — a merged view of HKLM\Software\Classes and HKCU\Software\Classes. HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC): current hardware profile info. Registry editor: regedit.exe. ALWAYS export (back up) a key before editing — File → Export — a bad registry edit can prevent Windows from booting.

prompt: A Windows 11 PC has widespread system instability. sfc /scannow reports it cannot repair some files. What should be run FIRST before trying sfc again?

options.text: chkdsk /r
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
format C: /fs:ntfs
diskpart

explanation: When sfc /scannow fails to repair files, it means the Windows Component Store (the source files sfc uses for replacement) is itself corrupted. DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) repairs the component store by downloading fresh files from Windows Update or a mounted image. Command: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. After DISM completes successfully, run sfc /scannow again — it can now use the repaired component store. Sequence: DISM first → sfc second. chkdsk /r: scans and repairs disk errors and bad sectors — separate from OS file corruption and unrelated to sfc failures. diskpart: partition management tool — not used for OS file repair.

prompt: A technician installs a new 6TB hard drive. After initializing in Disk Management with MBR style, only 2TB appears as usable space. How should this be fixed?

options.text: Format with FAT32 to access the full 6TB
Convert the disk to GPT partition style to support drives over 2TB
Split the drive into three 2TB volumes
Update the BIOS — MBR will then support 6TB

explanation: MBR (Master Boot Record) uses 32-bit LBA addressing and has a hard ceiling of 2TB. Any space beyond 2TB on an MBR disk is completely inaccessible and cannot be partitioned. Solution: convert to GPT (GUID Partition Table), which supports disks up to 9.4 ZB and up to 128 partitions on Windows. If the disk is empty: right-click in Disk Management → Convert to GPT Disk. If the disk has data: use MBR2GPT.exe (converts without data loss, requires Windows 10 1703+). GPT also requires UEFI firmware for bootable system drives. For any drive over 2TB — the answer is always GPT. FAT32 has a 2TB volume limit and a 4GB per-file limit — not a solution.

prompt: A technician suspects a recently installed device driver is causing system instability. Which Windows tool lets them view installed drivers, check device status, and roll back a driver?

options.text: Event Viewer
Device Manager
Disk Management
Services.msc

explanation: Device Manager (devmgmt.msc) is the go-to tool for hardware and driver management: view all detected hardware, see yellow exclamation marks for problematic devices, update drivers, roll back to a previous driver version, disable/enable devices, and uninstall devices. Driver rollback (Device Properties → Driver tab → Roll Back Driver) restores the previous driver — extremely useful when a new driver causes instability. Event Viewer: shows Windows system, application, and security logs — great for identifying WHAT went wrong (error messages, stop codes) but not for managing drivers. Disk Management: manages partitions and volumes. Services.msc: manages Windows services (start, stop, disable).

prompt: A macOS user needs to search for a file, launch an app, or perform a quick calculation without opening any application. Which macOS feature provides this?

options.text: Mission Control
Spotlight
FileVault
Keychain Access

explanation: macOS features tested on 220-1202: Spotlight (Cmd+Space): universal instant search — apps, files, emails, calendar, web results, unit conversions, math. Mission Control (Ctrl+Up arrow or 3-finger swipe up): shows all open windows, Spaces (virtual desktops), and full-screen apps — for window management. FileVault: macOS full-disk encryption using AES-128 — equivalent to Windows BitLocker. Requires recovery key backup. Time Machine: automated backup to external drive or network location — keeps hourly/daily/weekly snapshots. Keychain: macOS password/credential manager — stores Wi-Fi passwords, website logins, app credentials. Homebrew: community package manager for macOS — installs Unix/developer tools via command line.

prompt: A Linux administrator runs 'chmod 644 report.txt'. What permissions does this set on the file?

options.text: rwxrwxrwx — everyone has full access
rw-r--r-- — owner can read/write; group and others can read only
rwxr-xr-x — owner full; group/others read and execute
rw-rw-rw- — everyone can read and write

explanation: Linux permissions use octal notation: 4=read(r), 2=write(w), 1=execute(x). Three groups: owner, group, others. 644: 6(rw-)=owner read+write, 4(r--)=group read only, 4(r--)=others read only. Common permission values: 755 = rwxr-xr-x: standard for directories and executable scripts (owner full, others read+execute). 644 = rw-r--r--: standard for text/config files (owner read+write, others read only). 700 = rwx------: private to owner only. 777 = rwxrwxrwx: everyone full access — avoid on sensitive files/dirs. chmod command: chmod [octal] [file]. chown changes file ownership: chown user:group file. View permissions: ls -la shows the permission string in front of each file.

prompt: According to CompTIA's malware removal process, what is the SECOND step after identifying a malware infection?

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan with updated definitions
Quarantine the infected system by disconnecting it from the network
Format and reinstall the operating system
Change all user passwords from the infected machine

explanation: CompTIA 7-step malware removal process: 1. Investigate and verify malware symptoms. 2. QUARANTINE — isolate the system (disconnect network cable, disable Wi-Fi) to prevent lateral spread to other devices and cut the malware's connection to command-and-control servers. 3. Disable System Restore — malware can hide copies in restore points. 4. Remediate — boot to Safe Mode, update anti-malware definitions, run full scan, remove infections. 5. Schedule scans and run OS/software updates. 6. Re-enable System Restore and create a clean restore point. 7. Educate the user about how the infection occurred. Never change passwords from the infected machine — a keylogger may capture the new credentials.

prompt: A company is disposing of old SSDs containing sensitive customer data. A technician suggests degaussing the drives. Why is this approach INCORRECT for SSDs?

options.text: Degaussing is too expensive for SSDs
SSDs use NAND flash memory, not magnetic platters — degaussing has no effect on flash storage
Degaussing only works on USB drives, not M.2 SSDs
Degaussing requires the drive to be powered on

explanation: Degaussing works by applying an intense magnetic field to erase magnetically stored data — it is effective ONLY on magnetic media (HDDs, magnetic tape, floppy disks). SSDs store data in NAND flash memory chips using electrical charge — magnetic fields have absolutely no effect on them. For SSDs: Cryptographic erase — if the SSD uses self-encryption (SED/TCG Opal), destroying the encryption key makes all data mathematically unrecoverable. ATA Secure Erase — manufacturer-level command that resets all NAND cells. Physical destruction — shredding, disintegration, incineration — most absolute method. For HDDs: degaussing, overwriting (DoD 5220.22-M), or physical destruction. For compliance (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR): obtain a certificate of destruction.

prompt: An attacker calls an employee pretending to be from the corporate help desk, claims the employee's account was compromised, and urgently requests their current password to 'fix it.' This is BEST described as:

options.text: Phishing
Vishing
Smishing
Dumpster diving

explanation: Vishing (Voice phishing): social engineering attacks conducted via telephone or voice calls. The attacker impersonates a trusted authority (IT help desk, bank, IRS, tech support) to create urgency and manipulate the victim. Defense: IT departments have a policy of NEVER asking for passwords over the phone — train users to know this. Call-back verification: hang up and call the help desk's official number. Phishing: email-based. Smishing: SMS/text-based. Spear phishing: targeted phishing at a specific individual. Whaling: phishing targeting executives. Dumpster diving: physically searching trash for sensitive information. Pretexting: creating a fabricated scenario/identity to gain trust — vishing is a form of pretexting.

prompt: A security policy locks user accounts after 5 failed login attempts and requires an administrator to manually unlock them. What attack does this PRIMARILY prevent?

options.text: Phishing attacks
Brute force and password spray attacks
Physical tailgating
SQL injection

explanation: Account lockout policy prevents brute force attacks (trying many password combinations rapidly against one account) and password spray attacks (trying a few common passwords against many accounts). By locking after 5 failures, automated tools cannot systematically try thousands of passwords. Account lockout settings (Local Security Policy / Group Policy): Lockout threshold: number of bad attempts before lockout (5 is a common setting). Lockout duration: how long the account stays locked (0 = admin must unlock manually). Observation window: time window for counting failures. Trade-off: too aggressive lockout settings can cause denial-of-service (an attacker intentionally locks everyone out). Balance with reasonable thresholds. Complement with MFA for best protection.

prompt: Which Wi-Fi security protocol should a technician configure for BEST security on a small office wireless network in 2024?

options.text: WEP — strongest legacy encryption
WPA2-Personal with AES
WPA3-Personal with SAE
Open network — rely on VPN for security

explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which replaces WPA2's vulnerable PSK handshake. SAE provides: resistance to offline dictionary attacks (captured handshakes cannot be cracked offline), forward secrecy (past sessions cannot be decrypted even if the password is later discovered), protection against PMKID attacks. WEP: broken in minutes using free tools — never use. WPA (WPA1): deprecated, TKIP has known vulnerabilities. WPA2-Personal: still acceptable if WPA3 hardware is not available — use AES/CCMP mode, strong password (20+ random characters). WPA3 Transition Mode: supports both WPA2 and WPA3 clients simultaneously during hardware transition. For the 220-1202: WPA3 > WPA2 > WPA1 > WEP.

prompt: A user logs in with a password, then approves a push notification sent to their smartphone. Which MFA factor categories are being used?

options.text: Two knowledge factors — password and PIN
Something you know (password) and something you have (smartphone)
Something you are and something you know
Three factors — knowledge, possession, and location

explanation: Authentication factor categories: Something you KNOW: passwords, PINs, security questions, passphrases. Something you HAVE (possession): smartphone (authenticator app, push notification), hardware security key (YubiKey), smart card, OTP token, backup codes. Something you ARE (biometric/inherence): fingerprint, face scan, iris scan, voice recognition, behavioral biometrics. Somewhere you ARE: GPS location, IP geofencing — supplementary factor. True MFA requires two or more DIFFERENT categories. Password (know) + phone push (have) = two different categories = MFA. Password + PIN = two knowledge factors = NOT true MFA. Password + fingerprint = know + are = MFA. Hardware token (have) + PIN to unlock token (know) = MFA. The 220-1202 exam tests factor category identification.

prompt: When a standard user attempts to install software requiring admin rights on Windows, UAC prompts for administrator credentials. Which security principle does UAC implement?

options.text: Defense in depth
Least privilege
Separation of duties
Non-repudiation

explanation: UAC (User Account Control) enforces least privilege — users and processes run with the minimum privileges needed for everyday tasks. Even administrator accounts run as standard users by default; elevation is only granted when explicitly requested and approved. UAC levels: Always Notify (strictest — prompts for all changes). Notify for app changes (default — prompts when apps make changes, not for Windows settings). Notify without desktop dimming (less secure). Never notify (off — dangerous, malware can escalate without prompts). Disabling UAC removes this protection layer entirely. Least privilege principle: grant users/processes only the access they specifically need — nothing more. This limits blast radius if an account is compromised or malware runs under it.

prompt: A Windows workstation BSODs with stop code 0x0000000A (IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL) after installing a new USB hub driver. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The hard drive has bad sectors
The new USB driver has a bug causing improper memory access at an incorrect interrupt level
The user profile is corrupted
Windows Update failed to download

explanation: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (0x0000000A): a process or driver attempted to access a memory address at an IRQL (Interrupt Request Level) that was too high — almost always caused by a buggy, incompatible, or corrupted device driver. The timing (after installing a new USB hub driver) makes the culprit obvious. Fix: roll back the driver (Device Manager → USB Hub → Driver → Roll Back Driver) or uninstall the driver and download the updated version from the manufacturer. Other BSODs to know: 0x7B (INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE) = storage controller/BIOS change. 0x50 (PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA) = RAM failure. 0xEF (CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED) = core Windows process crash. BAD_POOL_HEADER = memory corruption.

prompt: Task Manager shows Windows disk usage at 100% constantly. The machine is a 3-year-old laptop with the original HDD. What should the technician check FIRST?

options.text: Increase the monitor refresh rate
Check SMART data for HDD health — a failing drive causes constant high disk activity
Update the graphics driver
Reinstall Windows immediately

explanation: Persistent 100% disk usage on an older mechanical HDD often indicates drive degradation — bad sectors cause repeated read retries, which show as constant disk activity. Check SMART (Self-Monitoring Analysis and Reporting Technology) data using tools like CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or smartctl (Linux) — look for Reallocated Sectors, Pending Sectors, or Uncorrectable Errors. Other 100% disk causes: Windows Update running (temporary — wait for completion), Search Indexing (initial setup — temporary), Superfetch/SysMain on low-RAM systems (disable if under 8GB), malware. Resource Monitor (resmon.exe) shows EXACTLY which process is causing disk activity — more detailed than Task Manager. An SSD upgrade dramatically improves performance on old laptops.

prompt: A user reports their browser homepage changed to an unknown site, new toolbars appeared, and searches redirect to unfamiliar engines. What malware type and remediation steps are indicated?

options.text: Ransomware — restore files from backup
Browser hijacker — remove extensions, reset browser, run anti-malware scan
Rootkit — boot from live CD and reinstall OS
Keylogger — change all passwords immediately

explanation: Browser hijackers modify browser settings — homepage, default search engine, new tab page — and install unwanted extensions or toolbars. Often bundled with free software (PUPs — Potentially Unwanted Programs). Remediation: 1. Remove suspicious extensions in browser settings. 2. Reset browser to defaults (Settings → Reset/Restore). 3. Check installed programs for unknown recent installations and uninstall them. 4. Run Malwarebytes or similar anti-malware (effective against PUPs and adware). 5. Check browser shortcut target for appended URLs. 6. Consider a full browser uninstall/reinstall for persistent cases. Ransomware: files locked, ransom demand note. Rootkit: deeply hidden, hard to detect, no obvious browser symptoms. Keylogger: silently records input, no visible browser changes.

prompt: A Windows 11 PC displays 'Winload.efi is missing or corrupt' and will not boot. What is the correct repair approach?

options.text: Run sfc /scannow from a command prompt in Windows
Boot from Windows installation media → Repair → Advanced Options → Startup Repair or bootrec commands
Use Disk Management to reformat the boot partition
Run chkdsk /f from within Windows

explanation: Winload.efi is the UEFI Windows boot loader — if missing or corrupt, Windows cannot start at all. Repair requires booting from external media (USB/DVD): Insert Windows installation media → Repair your computer → Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Repair (automatic) or Command Prompt (manual). Manual bootrec commands: bootrec /fixmbr (repairs MBR — legacy BIOS only). bootrec /fixboot (writes new boot sector). bootrec /rebuildbcd (rebuilds Boot Configuration Data — often fixes winload.efi). bcdboot C:\Windows /s C: (copies boot files, creates BCD). sfc /scannow cannot run before Windows boots — it requires a working OS environment. Startup Repair successfully handles the most common boot failures automatically.

prompt: A 2-year-old iPhone battery is swollen — the screen is slightly raised from the case. What action should the technician take?

options.text: Drain the battery completely and recharge to recalibrate
Stop using the device immediately — a swollen lithium battery is a fire/explosion hazard; replace professionally
Puncture the battery to release the buildup safely
Put the phone in the freezer to reduce swelling

explanation: A swollen (puffed) lithium battery is a critical safety hazard — the internal cells are producing gas from a chemical reaction (often from overcharging, heat damage, or age). A swollen battery is at risk of thermal runaway — it can rupture, release toxic gas, catch fire, or explode with significant force. Correct actions: Stop using the device immediately. Do not charge it further. Do not puncture, crush, or put in the microwave or freezer — these actions are dangerous. Take it to an authorized repair center for safe battery replacement and disposal. The repair tech must handle removal carefully — swollen batteries are fragile and must not be pierced or bent. Lithium battery fires burn intensely and require Class D or dry sand to extinguish — not water.

prompt: A user's spreadsheet application stops responding mid-task. The rest of the system is working fine. What is the QUICKEST way to terminate only the frozen application?

options.text: Hold the power button for 10 seconds
Ctrl+Shift+Esc → Task Manager → right-click frozen app → End Task
Run sfc /scannow to fix the application
Reinstall the application before trying again

explanation: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc is the direct shortcut — faster than Ctrl+Alt+Del → Task Manager) lets you selectively End Task only the frozen application without affecting anything else. Under the Processes tab, right-click the frozen app → End Task. Note: any unsaved work in the crashed application will be lost. Alternative if Task Manager won't open: Win+R → taskmgr. For deeper process analysis: Process Explorer (Sysinternals/Microsoft) shows process trees, DLL usage, and handles. Holding the power button reboots the entire system — loses all unsaved work in every open application. sfc repairs Windows system files — has no effect on third-party application crashes.

prompt: A user's Windows PC takes 5 minutes to boot and runs slowly afterward. Task Manager shows CPU at 15% but the startup tab shows 40 programs set to auto-start. What should the technician do?

options.text: Reinstall Windows to fix the performance issue
Disable unnecessary startup programs via Task Manager Startup tab or msconfig
Add more RAM before any other action
Defragment the hard drive as the first step

explanation: Excessive startup programs are a leading cause of slow boot times — each program initializes at startup, competing for disk I/O and CPU. Fix: Task Manager → Startup tab → right-click unneeded programs → Disable. Or: Win+R → msconfig → Startup tab (older Windows versions). Keep only essential programs (antivirus, cloud sync client, critical utilities) — disable everything else. Other performance tools: Disk Cleanup (cleanmgr.exe): removes temp files, old Windows updates. Storage Sense: automatic cleanup. Defrag: only for HDDs — SSDs should never be defragmented (it wears NAND flash). Prefetch/Superfetch: can cause disk thrashing on low-RAM systems. Check for malware — it often causes persistent slowness and may appear in startup entries.

prompt: A technician is about to install a RAM module into a desktop PC on a carpeted floor. What is the MOST important precaution to take?

options.text: Work quickly to minimize exposure time
Wear an anti-static wrist strap bonded to the PC chassis before handling components
Wear thick rubber gloves to insulate hands
Keep the RAM in the anti-static bag during installation

explanation: An anti-static wrist strap equalizes the electrical potential between the technician and the equipment — preventing electrostatic discharge (ESD) that can damage components invisibly. Bond the wrist strap to bare metal on the chassis (not a painted surface). Carpet is a major ESD generator — walking on carpet can build thousands of volts of static charge. Anti-static wrist strap: equalizes potential (most effective). Anti-static mat: dissipates charge from work surface (use together with strap). Anti-static bags: protect components in transit — remove component from bag AT the moment of installation, not before. Rubber gloves: INSULATE, do NOT prevent ESD — can actually build up charge. Speed does not reduce ESD risk. ESD damage can be latent — component works initially then fails prematurely.

prompt: A sysadmin needs to automatically create 200 user accounts in Active Directory from a CSV file. Which scripting tool is BEST suited for this on Windows?

options.text: Batch file (.bat) using net user commands
PowerShell (.ps1) using New-ADUser with Import-Csv
VBScript (.vbs) using WMI
Python script using subprocess module

explanation: PowerShell is purpose-built for Windows automation and Active Directory management. New-ADUser cmdlet creates AD accounts; Import-Csv reads the CSV file; a simple ForEach loop processes all 200 rows. Example: Import-Csv users.csv | ForEach-Object { New-ADUser -Name $_.Name -UserPrincipalName $_.UPN ... }. PowerShell advantages for AD: native Active Directory module, structured objects (not just text), runs remotely, manages Azure AD, integrates with Microsoft 365, extensive cmdlet library. Batch files: basic Windows scripting — cannot natively manage Active Directory. VBScript: older Microsoft scripting, being deprecated. Python: powerful but requires additional modules for AD management and is not natively integrated with Windows AD management tooling.

prompt: A help desk technician needs to remotely view and control a user's Windows desktop to troubleshoot an issue. The user is on the corporate network. Which port must be open for Windows Remote Desktop?

options.text: Port 22 (SSH)
Port 5900 (VNC)
Port 3389 (RDP)
Port 443 (HTTPS)

explanation: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) uses TCP port 3389. Requirements: Windows Pro or higher on the target PC, RDP enabled (System Properties → Remote → Allow connections), connecting user has permission, firewall rule allows port 3389. Security best practices: expose RDP only through VPN, not directly to the internet (RDP on internet = major attack surface). Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA). Consider changing default port from 3389 (security through obscurity, minor benefit). Restrict who can RDP via Group Policy. Port comparison: SSH = 22 (text-based terminal, Linux/network devices). VNC = 5900 (graphical, cross-platform, less secure by default). HTTPS = 443 (web, also used by some remote tools like TeamViewer through NAT).

prompt: Before deploying a major Windows update across 500 corporate workstations, an IT team creates step-by-step instructions for reverting to the previous state if the update causes widespread issues. What document is this?

options.text: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
Rollback plan
Network diagram
Acceptable Use Policy

explanation: A rollback plan (backout plan) documents exactly how to undo a change if it fails — step-by-step, specific commands, who is responsible. It is a required component of proper change management. CompTIA change management flow: 1. Documented business reason. 2. Risk and impact analysis. 3. Change Advisory Board (CAB) approval. 4. Create rollback plan BEFORE implementing. 5. Schedule maintenance window. 6. Implement (test in non-production first). 7. Verify success. 8. Document results. Without a rollback plan: a failed deployment affecting 500 machines could take days to remediate. With a rollback plan: reverting is structured and fast. SLA: service availability guarantee between provider and customer. AUP: Acceptable Use Policy — defines appropriate computer use for employees.

prompt: A server room contains expensive equipment and uses a Novec 1230 clean agent fire suppression system. What is the primary advantage of a clean agent system over water sprinklers in this environment?

options.text: Clean agents are cheaper to install
Clean agents are required by the NEC for all IT rooms
Clean agents suppress fires without damaging electronics or leaving conductive residue
Water sprinklers cannot extinguish electrical fires

explanation: Clean agent fire suppression systems (Novec 1230, FM-200/HFC-227ea, Inergen, CO2) extinguish fires by removing heat or displacing oxygen without water. Benefits for data centers: zero water damage, no conductive residue, electronics can potentially survive a suppression event, minimal cleanup. Water sprinklers: would destroy servers, storage arrays, and networking equipment even if the fire itself was minor. CO2 systems: very effective but dangerous to people (displaces oxygen) — areas must be evacuated BEFORE discharge; not suitable for occupied spaces. Halon: the original clean agent — very effective but ozone-depleting, globally phased out under the Montreal Protocol. For electrical fires with a portable extinguisher: use Class C (dry chemical) but expect residue damage to electronics.

prompt: After resolving a rare but complex issue where a specific model of laptop loses Wi-Fi after sleep due to a power management setting, what should the technician create to help the entire support team?

options.text: A purchase order for newer laptops
A knowledge base article documenting the symptoms, root cause, and exact fix steps
A change request to disable sleep on all laptops
An email to the user explaining the fix

explanation: Knowledge base articles (KBAs) convert individual troubleshooting experience into reusable team knowledge. A complex 2-hour diagnosis becomes a 2-minute fix for any subsequent technician who searches the KB. Good KBA structure: Symptoms (exactly what the user reports), Affected hardware/software versions, Root cause, Step-by-step resolution, Any preventive measures, Author and date. Documentation the 220-1202 tests: Physical network diagram (cable runs, room locations), Logical diagram (IP addressing, VLANs, routing), Asset inventory (hardware/software), Knowledge base, Ticketing system records, Change log, SOP (Standard Operating Procedure), AUP (Acceptable Use Policy). Always document — it's faster the second time and enables team knowledge sharing.

prompt: A technician needs to map a network share (\\fileserver\data) to drive letter Z: for a user. Which command accomplishes this?

options.text: net use Z: \\fileserver\data
ipconfig /all
nslookup fileserver
netstat -an

explanation: net use maps network drives from the CLI: net use Z: \\fileserver\data. To persist across reboots add /persistent:yes. To map with credentials: add /user:DOMAIN\username. To disconnect: net use Z: /delete. Other net commands to know for 220-1202: net user — manage user accounts. net accounts — view password and lockout policies. net localgroup — manage local groups. net share — view or create shares. net start/stop — start or stop Windows services.

prompt: An administrator wants a script to run automatically every Sunday night at 2 AM. Which Windows tool should be used?

options.text: Services.msc
Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc)
Event Viewer
msconfig

explanation: Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc) creates automated tasks triggered by: time/schedule (daily, weekly, one-time), system events (startup, logon, Event Log entry), or idle time. For Sunday 2 AM: Create Task → Triggers → New → Weekly, Sunday, 2:00 AM. Actions tab: Start a Program, browse to the script. Common uses: backup scripts, software updates, log cleanup, report generation. Services.msc: manages Windows services — not for scheduling time-based tasks. Event Viewer: reads log files — does not schedule tasks. msconfig: controls startup programs and boot options, not scheduled tasks.

prompt: A Linux administrator needs to find all lines containing the word ‘error’ (case-insensitive) in a file called syslog.txt. Which command is CORRECT?

options.text: find syslog.txt -name error
grep -i error syslog.txt
ls -la syslog.txt
cat syslog.txt | sort

explanation: grep searches for patterns in files. The -i flag makes the search case-insensitive (matches Error, ERROR, error). grep -r error /var/log/: recursively searches all files in a directory. grep -v error syslog.txt: inverts match — shows lines that do NOT contain ‘error’. grep -n: shows line numbers. grep -c: shows count of matching lines. Piping: journalctl | grep error filters journalctl output for errors. Other Linux commands: cat (display file), less/more (paginate), tail -f (follow log in real-time), sort (alphabetically sort), wc -l (count lines).

prompt: A user needs to check which Windows services are set to start automatically and which are currently stopped. Which tool provides this most directly?

options.text: Task Manager, Processes tab
Services.msc (services console)
Device Manager
Disk Management

explanation: Services.msc displays all Windows services with their current status (Running, Stopped, Paused) and startup type (Automatic, Automatic Delayed Start, Manual, Disabled). From here an admin can start/stop/restart services, change startup type, and configure recovery actions. Startup types: Automatic starts at boot; Automatic Delayed Start starts after boot completes (reduces boot time); Manual starts only when called by another process or user; Disabled cannot start at all. Task Manager Processes tab shows running processes and resource usage in real-time — does not show stopped services or startup types. PowerShell: Get-Service lists services with status.

prompt: A Mac user wants to see all currently running applications and background processes and kill an unresponsive one. Which macOS tool is equivalent to Windows Task Manager?

options.text: Spotlight
Activity Monitor
Disk Utility
Keychain Access

explanation: Activity Monitor (Applications → Utilities) is macOS’s equivalent of Windows Task Manager. It shows CPU usage per process, RAM usage and memory pressure, Energy impact (battery), Disk read/write activity, and Network traffic per process. To force quit an unresponsive app: select it → click the X button. Quick alternative: Cmd+Option+Esc opens the Force Quit Applications window. Other macOS tools: Disk Utility: manage disks, format, repair. System Information: hardware inventory. Console: macOS log viewer (equivalent to Event Viewer). Terminal: command-line interface. Keychain Access: credential and certificate management.

prompt: A company needs to deploy Windows 11 Pro to 200 laptops without manual installation on each device. Which method enables centralized automated deployment?

options.text: Manually installing from USB on each laptop
Windows Deployment Services (WDS) or MDT with network boot (PXE)
Downloading Windows Update on each laptop individually
Copying the C: drive from one laptop to all others via USB

explanation: PXE (Preboot eXecution Environment) boot lets computers boot from a network server instead of local media. WDS or MDT hosts Windows images pushed to PXE-booting client machines. Administrators create a sysprep-prepared image stored on the server; clients pull it automatically — fully automated with no manual interaction per device. Additional tools: Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM/SCCM) for enterprise deployment. Autopilot: cloud-based, uses existing OEM Windows install and configures it via Azure AD enrollment. Unattended installation: answer file (unattend.xml) automates installation questions. Copying a C: drive without sysprep creates SID conflicts and licensing issues on domain environments.

prompt: A building uses key card access to enter secure server rooms with logging of every entry attempt. Which physical security control supports this logging requirement?

options.text: Security guards stationed at every door
Electronic key card system with audit logging
Mechanical combination locks
Window bars and reinforced doors

explanation: Electronic key card (badge) systems log every access event: user ID, door location, timestamp, and success/failure. This creates an audit trail for security investigations, compliance, and accountability. Mechanical combination locks: shared combination with no audit trail (no way to know who entered or when). Mantrap (airlock): physically allows only one person through at a time, preventing tailgating. For compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA), electronic access control with logging is required for physical access to systems handling regulated data. Access logs should be stored securely and reviewed regularly for anomalies.

prompt: A company policy requires passwords to be at least 14 characters with complexity requirements and change every 90 days. Where are these requirements enforced on a standalone Windows machine?

options.text: Device Manager
Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) → Account Policies → Password Policy
Task Scheduler
Event Viewer

explanation: Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) configures: Password Policy (minimum length, complexity, maximum age, history), Account Lockout Policy (lockout threshold, duration, observation window), and local auditing settings. On domain-joined machines, Group Policy Objects (GPOs) from Active Directory override local security policy. To access: Win+R → secpol.msc, or Control Panel → Administrative Tools → Local Security Policy. Password complexity: when enabled, requires at least 3 of 4 character types (uppercase, lowercase, numbers, special characters) and cannot contain the username. PowerShell alternative: Get-LocalUser, Set-LocalUser cmdlets.

prompt: A user downloads a free game from a website and their antivirus does not alert. The next day, unauthorized purchases appear on their credit card. Which threat MOST likely slipped past the antivirus?

options.text: A signature-based virus that is well-known
A Trojan or spyware bundled with the game that is too new to have a signature
A physical keylogger hardware device
A DDoS attack targeting the user’s computer

explanation: Traditional signature-based antivirus cannot detect NEW malware that has not been analyzed and added to signature databases. A Trojan disguised as a free game (a very common attack vector) that is newly deployed evades signature detection. Spyware or keylogger components then capture payment credentials. Defense layers: real-time behavior-based detection (EDR) catches suspicious actions. SmartScreen Filter: warns about unsigned or low-reputation downloads. Reputation-based protection: blocks downloads with few installs globally. User education: download only from reputable sources, prefer app stores. Enable automatic definition updates to minimize the window of signature-less vulnerability.

prompt: An organization needs to dispose of old laptops containing sensitive financial data on SATA SSDs. Which disposal method BEST ensures data is unrecoverable for compliance purposes?

options.text: Delete all files and empty the Recycle Bin
Format the SSD using the Windows format command
Perform ATA Secure Erase or cryptographic erase and obtain a certificate of destruction
Degauss all the SSDs

explanation: Standard deletion and even formatting do NOT securely erase SSDs. The file system is updated to mark space as free but data remains physically on the NAND chips and is recoverable with forensic tools. Secure methods for SSDs: ATA Secure Erase — a built-in SATA command resetting all NAND cells to factory state. Cryptographic Erase — if the SSD uses self-encryption (SED), destroy the encryption key and all data becomes unreadable instantly. Physical Destruction — shredding or disintegration, required for the highest classification data. Certificate of Destruction: a legal document from a certified disposal vendor proving secure disposal — required for HIPAA, PCI DSS, and enterprise audits. Degaussing is effective ONLY on magnetic (HDD) media — completely ineffective on SSDs.

prompt: A third-party business application crashes every time it starts on one specific Windows 11 workstation but works fine on other machines. What are the BEST initial troubleshooting steps?

options.text: Immediately reinstall Windows 11 on the affected workstation
Check Event Viewer for application crash errors, verify runtime prerequisites, and try running as administrator
Replace the monitor on the affected workstation
Update the BIOS firmware and GPU driver

explanation: Application crash troubleshooting: 1) Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) → Windows Logs → Application: look for Error events at the crash time, noting the Faulting Module (missing DLL, incompatible runtime). 2) Check prerequisites: missing or wrong version of .NET Framework, Visual C++ Runtime, DirectX, or Java are a leading cause. 3) Run as Administrator: UAC or permission issues can crash apps that need elevated access. 4) Compare differences from working machines: OS version, same prerequisites, antivirus exclusions. 5) Try Compatibility mode: right-click app → Properties → Compatibility. The crash being machine-specific points to a local software difference, not a bug in the application itself.

prompt: A user opens an email attachment and suddenly sees a full-screen demand for cryptocurrency to decrypt their files. Files now have unusual extensions. What is the FIRST action to take?

options.text: This is a scareware pop-up — close the browser and run antivirus
Ransomware has encrypted the user’s files. FIRST: disconnect from the network immediately to prevent spread to shared drives and other machines
Pay the ransom immediately to restore files quickly
Restart the computer to interrupt the encryption process

explanation: Ransomware encrypts victim files and demands payment for the decryption key. File extension changes confirm actual encryption (not just scareware). FIRST action: isolate immediately — disconnect from the network (unplug Ethernet, disable Wi-Fi). Ransomware actively seeks and encrypts network shares, backup drives, and connected systems. Every second of connectivity means more files encrypted. Then: Report to IT security/incident response team. Do NOT pay the ransom (FBI recommendation) — no guarantee of receiving a working decryption key, and it funds criminal operations. Check backup integrity. Identify the ransomware variant at IDRansomware.malwarehunterteam.com — a free decryptor may exist for some strains. Restarting does not stop encryption and may complicate forensics.

prompt: A Windows 11 PC displays ‘Operating System not found’ after BIOS POST. The drive is detected in BIOS. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The CPU is overheating
The boot partition is missing, corrupted, or the Boot Configuration Data (BCD) is damaged
The RAM failed
The display driver is corrupt

explanation: ‘Operating System not found’ after BIOS POST with the drive detected means the BIOS can see the disk but cannot find a valid bootable partition. Causes: BCD corruption, MBR/GPT damage, boot partition missing or deleted, or wrong boot order. Repair steps: boot from Windows installation media → Repair your computer → Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Command Prompt. Commands to try: bootrec /fixmbr (repairs the Master Boot Record), bootrec /fixboot (writes a new boot sector), bootrec /rebuildbcd (scans for Windows installations and rebuilds BCD), bcdboot C:\Windows (copies boot files). If on a GPT disk, ensure UEFI mode is active in BIOS (not legacy BIOS/CSM mode).

prompt: A smartphone became extremely slow, apps crash frequently, and battery drains within 2 hours. All symptoms appeared suddenly yesterday. What should be done FIRST?

options.text: Immediately perform a factory reset
Check recently installed apps — a new app may be causing excessive resource usage; verify battery usage stats in Settings
Replace the battery
Update the carrier SIM card

explanation: The sudden onset of symptoms after a period of normal operation strongly suggests a recently installed or updated app is the culprit. Steps: 1) Check Settings → Battery → Battery Usage: identify which app consumes excessive battery. 2) Check Settings → Apps: look for any recently installed app. 3) Uninstall recently installed apps one by one and test after each removal. An app with a runaway background process drains battery and slows the device. A factory reset erases all data and is a last resort — try removing suspect apps first. Battery replacement is not indicated since the battery was working well until recently.

prompt: A Windows PC runs very slow. Task Manager shows Windows Defender Antivirus Service consuming 90% CPU continuously. What should the technician check FIRST?

options.text: Disable Windows Defender permanently
Uninstall Windows 11 and install Windows 10
Check if a full scan is in progress, schedule scans during off-hours, or investigate if Defender is scanning a problematic file in a loop
Replace the CPU

explanation: Windows Defender performs scheduled full scans that consume significant CPU during the scan. Solutions: 1) Check the Defender dashboard — is a scan actively running? If so, pause it or let it finish. 2) Schedule scans for off-hours: Windows Security → Virus & Threat Protection → scan schedule settings. 3) Check if Defender is repeatedly scanning one file causing a loop — add that path to exclusions if the file is known-safe. 4) Ensure Defender definitions are up-to-date (outdated definitions can increase scanning effort). Disabling Defender completely is a security risk. Windows Update running simultaneously can also cause high CPU and disk usage that may be mistakenly attributed to Defender.

prompt: After a ransomware attack, an IT team tries to restore from backup but discovers the backup files are also encrypted. What backup design failure caused this?

options.text: The backup software was running on Windows
The backup destination was a network share accessible from the infected machine, allowing ransomware to encrypt the backup too
The backup schedule was set to weekly
The backup hardware was not fast enough

explanation: Ransomware actively seeks and encrypts all reachable storage: local drives, mapped drives, and accessible network shares. If backup destination shares are mounted on or reachable from infected machines, ransomware encrypts them too. Backup architecture best practices: Offline backups — media physically disconnected from the network (tape, external drive rotated offsite). Immutable backups — cloud or NAS features preventing modification or deletion even by authenticated accounts. Air-gapped backups — backup systems with no network path to production systems. 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 copy offsite. The offsite or offline copy is the one that survives ransomware. Test restores regularly — untested backups frequently fail when needed most.

prompt: A server room has a UPS providing battery backup. Why should servers NOT be plugged into standard power strips connected to the UPS output?

options.text: Power strips cannot handle the voltage from a UPS
Standard power strips may not support the combined amperage of server power supplies and daisy-chaining strips violates electrical code
UPS units only support one connected device
Power strips disable the UPS battery backup feature

explanation: Daisy-chaining power strips off a UPS introduces risks: power strips may have total amperage limits below the combined load of multiple servers, causing overheating or tripping. Standard power strips lack individual outlet surge protection. Daisy-chaining power strips is also an electrical code violation (NEC) in many jurisdictions. Best practice: use a Power Distribution Unit (PDU) specifically designed for data center use, connected directly to the UPS. PDUs are rated for data center loads and provide individual circuit protection and monitoring. UPS runtime calculation: divide UPS capacity (VA) by connected load (W) to estimate runtime — always check the manufacturer’s runtime charts for accurate estimates at different load levels.

prompt: A help desk technician needs to remotely view and control a user’s desktop to resolve an issue without requiring admin rights from the user. Which tool shares the user’s CURRENT active session?

options.text: SSH
Remote Desktop (RDP) — requires Windows Pro and creates a separate session
Windows Quick Assist or Remote Assistance — the user shares their active session with a help code
FTP

explanation: Windows Quick Assist (Windows 10/11, free, built-in) and Remote Assistance (older Windows) allow an end user to share their CURRENT desktop session with a helper. The user initiates the session with a code, requiring no admin rights. Quick Assist: a simple 6-digit code, works through most firewalls via Microsoft relay servers, ideal for help desk. Remote Desktop (RDP): requires the target machine to be Windows Pro+ with RDP enabled, and creates a NEW separate session — the user sees their session locked. This is not ideal for watching what the user is experiencing. Third-party tools: TeamViewer, AnyDesk, Zoom remote control, and ConnectWise ScreenConnect offer cross-platform remote support. SSH: text-based command line only, no graphical desktop control.

prompt: After resolving a network outage caused by a misconfigured VLAN setting, a technician should do which of the following BEFORE closing the ticket?

options.text: Send an invoice to the affected department
Document the root cause, resolution steps, preventive measures, and resolution time in the ticketing system
Delete all related logs to prevent a security exposure
Update only the status field to ‘Closed’ and move on

explanation: Proper incident documentation should capture: Incident description and symptoms. Diagnosis process and findings (what was wrong, why it happened). Resolution steps taken (exactly what was done). Root cause analysis (what caused the misconfiguration). Preventive measures (what will be done to avoid recurrence). Affected systems, duration of outage, impact on users. Time to resolution for MTTR tracking. Good documentation enables: knowledge base articles for future similar incidents, trend analysis, accountability, audit trails for compliance, and faster resolution next time by different technicians. Never delete logs — they are part of the audit trail. Only updating the Status field with no detail is an incomplete closure that fails the organization.

prompt: A technician tries to upgrade a 2019 desktop to Windows 11 but the setup wizard blocks the installation. Which TWO hardware requirements are UNIQUE to Windows 11 and not required by Windows 10?

options.text: 2 GHz dual-core CPU and 8 GB RAM
TPM 2.0 chip and UEFI Secure Boot support
At least 500 GB hard drive and USB 3.0 ports
Dedicated GPU and DirectX 12 Ultimate support

explanation: Windows 11 has two hardware requirements that Windows 10 does NOT enforce: TPM 2.0 (Trusted Platform Module) must be present and enabled in BIOS/UEFI, and Secure Boot must be supported by the firmware. Other requirements are modest: 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage, 1 GHz processor, DirectX 12 GPU. Check compatibility: run the PC Health Check app, or check tpm.msc (TPM version) and msinfo32 (BIOS Mode must show UEFI, not Legacy). Machines with only TPM 1.2 or Legacy BIOS mode fail Windows 11 eligibility. Most CPUs from 2018 or newer on supported chipsets qualify for the upgrade.

prompt: A technician adds a registry entry that stores a numeric timeout value for a software application. Which registry value type is the correct choice for a 32-bit unsigned integer?

options.text: REG_SZ
REG_DWORD
REG_BINARY
REG_EXPAND_SZ

explanation: REG_DWORD stores a 32-bit (4-byte) unsigned integer and is used for numeric settings such as enable/disable flags (0 or 1), port numbers, timeouts, and similar values. REG_QWORD handles 64-bit integers for larger numbers. REG_SZ holds a simple null-terminated string for text values like file paths. REG_EXPAND_SZ is a string that supports environment-variable references such as %SystemRoot%. REG_BINARY stores raw binary data used for hardware settings and certificates. REG_MULTI_SZ is a list of strings separated by null characters. Memorize REG_SZ (string), REG_DWORD (32-bit int), REG_BINARY (binary data), and REG_EXPAND_SZ (expandable string) for the 220-1202 exam.

prompt: A Windows 11 PC enters a continuous reboot loop before the login screen appears. Which startup option loads only essential drivers so a technician can diagnose the problem?

options.text: Startup Repair
Safe Mode
Last Known Good Configuration
WinRE Command Prompt

explanation: Safe Mode boots Windows with only the minimum essential drivers and services, excluding third-party drivers, startup programs, and (in basic Safe Mode) networking. If the system boots in Safe Mode but not normally, the cause is a third-party driver, startup program, or service. Access Safe Mode by holding Shift while clicking Restart, then Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Settings → F4 (Safe Mode) or F5 (Safe Mode with Networking). Alternatively use msconfig → Boot tab → Safe Boot checkbox. Safe Mode with Networking adds network drivers and is useful when updates or online tools are needed for repair.

prompt: A USB drive must store individual files larger than 4 GB and work natively on both Windows and macOS without extra software. Which file system meets both requirements?

options.text: FAT32
NTFS
exFAT
ext4

explanation: exFAT (Extended FAT) supports files larger than 4 GB and is natively readable and writable on Windows, macOS, and modern Linux, making it ideal for USB drives shared across operating systems. FAT32 has a hard 4 GB per-file limit regardless of drive size, and Windows also caps FAT32 formatting at 32 GB. NTFS supports large files and permissions but macOS can only read NTFS drives natively, not write to them without third-party software. ext4 is the standard Linux file system; Windows cannot access it without additional drivers. For cross-platform external storage, exFAT is the modern standard.

prompt: A Windows workstation with 8 GB RAM runs slowly and Task Manager shows RAM at 95% with heavy disk activity. What is happening and what is the best long-term fix?

options.text: Windows is defragmenting the paging file — disable paging
Windows is using virtual memory (paging file) because physical RAM is exhausted — adding more RAM is the best fix
The Memory Compression process is malware — quarantine it
Windows is encrypting RAM with BitLocker — disable BitLocker

explanation: When physical RAM is exhausted, Windows uses a paging file (pagefile.sys) on the disk to extend apparent memory by swapping less-used pages. Disk storage is far slower than RAM, so heavy paging causes severe performance degradation. Memory Compression, visible in Task Manager, is a legitimate Windows feature that compresses in-memory pages before they are written to the paging file to reduce disk I/O. The best fix is adding more physical RAM. As a temporary measure, the paging file size can be increased via System → Advanced System Settings → Performance Settings → Advanced → Virtual Memory. On SSDs the performance penalty is lower than on HDDs, but RAM is still far faster than any storage device.

prompt: A technician needs to completely erase all partitions on a USB drive and create a single new formatted partition using only Windows built-in command-line tools. Which DiskPart sequence is correct?

options.text: format → partition → active
list disk → select disk → clean → create partition primary → format fs=fat32 quick → assign
fdisk → mkfs → mount
chkdsk → sfc → diskpart

explanation: The correct DiskPart sequence is: open diskpart, then list disk to identify the correct drive number, select disk X (replace X carefully — wrong disk causes irreversible data loss), clean to remove all partition and volume information, create partition primary to use all available space, format fs=fat32 quick (or ntfs for Windows-only use), and assign to automatically assign a drive letter. The clean command is irreversible and wipes the disk immediately without confirmation, so verifying the disk number first is critical. Adding all before clean (clean all) overwrites every sector with zeros for a more thorough erase but takes much longer.

prompt: A Linux administrator needs to locate application configuration files system-wide and a specific user's personal documents. Which directories contain these respectively?

options.text: /bin for configs and /root for personal documents
/etc for system configuration files and /home/username for personal documents
/var for configs and /tmp for documents
/usr for configs and /dev for documents

explanation: The Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) defines: /etc holds system-wide configuration files such as sshd_config, passwd, fstab, hosts, and nginx.conf. /home contains user home directories — each user has a subdirectory /home/username with their personal files, Desktop, Downloads, and shell config files. /bin and /usr/bin hold user-executable programs. /var holds variable data including log files (/var/log), mail spools, and web content. /tmp holds temporary files cleared on reboot. /dev contains device files representing hardware. /root is the home directory of the root superuser only, not regular users. /opt stores optional third-party software packages.

prompt: A technician needs to install the curl utility on an Ubuntu Server. Which command correctly installs it using Ubuntu's native package manager?

options.text: yum install curl
apt install curl
brew install curl
zypper install curl

explanation: Ubuntu and Debian-based distributions use apt (Advanced Package Tool). The correct command is: sudo apt update (refresh the package list), then sudo apt install curl. Red Hat, CentOS, and Fedora use yum (older) or dnf (newer). SUSE and openSUSE use zypper. Homebrew (brew) is a third-party package manager for macOS, not a Linux system tool. Arch Linux uses pacman. Always run apt update before installing on Debian-based systems to ensure the package list is current. For the 220-1202 exam: apt — Ubuntu/Debian; yum/dnf — Red Hat/CentOS.

prompt: A Linux administrator sees a process with PID 1847 consuming 98% CPU in the top utility. What is the correct command to immediately and forcefully terminate it?

options.text: delete 1847
stop mysqld
kill -9 1847
end -f 1847

explanation: The kill command sends signals to processes. kill PID sends SIGTERM (signal 15), which requests a graceful shutdown and allows the process to clean up. kill -9 PID sends SIGKILL, which immediately and forcefully terminates the process without any cleanup — use this when the process does not respond to SIGTERM. killall process_name kills all processes matching the given name. pkill pattern kills processes by name pattern. From within top, press k, then enter the PID to kill a process interactively. ps aux | grep process_name is used to find a PID by name before killing it. SIGKILL cannot be intercepted, blocked, or ignored by the target process.

prompt: A macOS user needs to view a hidden configuration file (dot file) directly in Finder without using Terminal. What keyboard shortcut toggles hidden file visibility in a Finder window?

options.text: Cmd+H
Cmd+Shift+Period
Cmd+Shift+H
Ctrl+Alt+H

explanation: In macOS Finder, pressing Cmd+Shift+Period (the period key) toggles the display of hidden files on and off. Files and folders whose names begin with a period (dot files) such as .bashrc, .ssh, .gitconfig, and .zshrc are hidden by default. This shortcut provides a quick toggle without using Terminal. The permanent Terminal command is: defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles YES, followed by killall Finder to restart Finder. Cmd+H hides the currently active application window. Cmd+Shift+G opens the Go to Folder dialog for typing a path directly. Cmd+I shows the Get Info panel for a selected item.

prompt: A macOS user downloads a utility from a developer's website (not the App Store) and sees: 'App cannot be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software.' Which feature is causing this and how can the user safely bypass it for a trusted app?

options.text: FileVault is blocking the file — decrypt the drive first
Gatekeeper is blocking the unsigned or unnotarized app — override it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway
The download is corrupted — re-download and retry
App Sandbox is preventing execution — disable it in Terminal

explanation: Gatekeeper is a macOS security feature that verifies apps have a valid Apple Developer signature and have been notarized (scanned by Apple for malware) before they are allowed to run. Apps from the Mac App Store always pass. Apps from identified developers that are notarized pass automatically. Apps from unrecognized or unsigned developers are blocked. To allow a trusted app that Gatekeeper blocked: open System Settings (or System Preferences) → Privacy & Security → scroll to the Security section → click Open Anyway next to the blocked app name. Alternatively, right-click (Control-click) the app in Finder → Open → click Open in the dialog that appears. This adds an exception only for this specific app.

prompt: An IT administrator needs to enforce an automatic screen lock after 10 minutes of inactivity on all Windows workstations in an Active Directory domain. What is the most efficient method?

options.text: Log in to each workstation and configure the screensaver locally in secpol.msc
Create a Group Policy Object (GPO) in Active Directory and link it to the OU containing the workstations
Email all users asking them to configure their own screen locks
Use Task Scheduler on each PC to run a lock script at login

explanation: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) allow a single configuration to be applied to all targeted domain-joined computers simultaneously. The screensaver lock is configured at: User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Control Panel → Personalization. Enable Screen Saver, set the timeout to 600 seconds (10 minutes), enable Password protect the screen saver, and optionally force a specific screensaver. Once applied, users cannot modify these settings because the controls are grayed out. GPOs refresh automatically every 90 minutes and at login, or immediately with gpupdate /force. This is far more efficient than configuring each machine individually and ensures consistent enforcement across the organization.

prompt: After installing a new application, a Windows 11 PC becomes unstable. The user wants to undo the changes without reinstalling Windows or losing personal files. Which Windows feature should be used?

options.text: Reset this PC (removes all apps and settings)
System Restore (reverts system files and registry to a prior restore point)
Refresh Windows (reinstalls Windows keeping personal files)
Startup Repair (only fixes boot issues)

explanation: System Restore reverts system files, the Windows registry, and installed programs to a saved restore point without affecting personal files such as documents and photos. Restore points are created automatically before Windows Updates, driver installations, and major software installs, and can also be created manually. Access it via Control Panel → System → System Protection → System Restore, or by typing rstrui.exe in the Run dialog. It is also accessible from Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) if Windows does not boot normally. System Protection must be enabled for restore points to be created — verify this before relying on System Restore. It does not recover deleted user files and is not a substitute for a data backup.

prompt: A user running Windows 10 Home wants to access BitLocker and domain join features. They need to move to Windows 11 Pro. What is the correct upgrade path?

options.text: Direct in-place upgrade from Windows 10 Home to Windows 11 Pro using a Pro product key or the Microsoft Store
Must first upgrade to Windows 10 Pro, then upgrade to Windows 11 Pro
Windows 10 Home cannot be upgraded to any Windows 11 edition
Must perform a clean install — in-place upgrades between editions are not supported

explanation: Windows 10 Home can be upgraded directly to Windows 11 Pro without an intermediate step through Windows 10 Pro. The upgrade can be performed by purchasing a Windows 11 Pro license key through the Microsoft Store (Settings → System → Activation → Change product key), or by running the Windows 11 setup media and entering a Pro key. In-place upgrades preserve personal files, installed applications, and settings. A clean install wipes everything and is used when a fresh start is preferred or when an in-place upgrade fails. Downgrading from Pro to Home always requires a clean install. Windows 11 Home does not include BitLocker full-disk encryption or Active Directory domain join — both require Pro or higher.

prompt: A Windows Server rebooted unexpectedly at 3 AM with no scheduled maintenance. Which tool and log should the administrator check first to find the root cause?

options.text: Task Manager — check CPU usage history
Event Viewer → Windows Logs → System — look for critical or error events around 3 AM
Device Manager — check for failed devices
Disk Management — review partition health

explanation: Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) is the primary Windows diagnostic log tool. The System log records hardware events, driver failures, service events, and unexpected reboots. Key event IDs for unexpected reboots: Event ID 41 (Kernel-Power) indicates a system reboot without a clean shutdown — the most important indicator. Event ID 6008 records an unexpected shutdown. Event ID 1074 records a planned shutdown or restart. To investigate: open Event Viewer → Windows Logs → System → Filter Current Log → select Critical and Error levels → set the time range to around 3 AM. Look for the critical event immediately before the reboot timestamp to identify the triggering cause.

prompt: A technician installs a new 2 TB SSD that is visible in BIOS but does not appear in File Explorer. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Reinstall Windows to detect the new drive
Open Disk Management, initialize the disk with GPT, create a new simple volume, and format it
Run chkdsk on the new drive
Update the storage controller driver

explanation: A brand-new drive is uninitialized and has no file system, so File Explorer cannot display it. The process is: open Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc or right-click Start → Disk Management). The disk appears as Unknown — Not Initialized. Right-click the disk → Initialize Disk → choose GPT (recommended for modern systems and drives over 2 TB). Right-click the unallocated space → New Simple Volume. Follow the wizard: set volume size, assign a drive letter, choose NTFS (recommended for internal drives), and perform a quick format. The volume then appears in File Explorer. Uninitialized drives appear in Disk Management but not in File Explorer because File Explorer only shows formatted volumes with assigned drive letters.

prompt: BitLocker is configured on a laptop. What role does the TPM chip play in protecting the drive?

options.text: The TPM permanently stores the encryption key, eliminating the need for any PIN
The TPM seals the BitLocker key and releases it only when boot measurements match expected values, blocking access if the drive is moved to another machine
The TPM provides the AES encryption engine used for disk I/O
The TPM automatically backs up the recovery key to Azure

explanation: The TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is a dedicated security chip that seals cryptographic keys to specific platform state. During each boot, the TPM records SHA-256 hashes of the firmware, bootloader, and other boot components into Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs). The BitLocker encryption key is sealed to expected PCR values. If the boot chain changes — for example, a new drive is inserted, the firmware is modified, or the disk is moved to a different machine — the PCR values differ from the sealed values and the TPM refuses to release the key. Windows then prompts for the 48-digit BitLocker recovery key. This prevents offline attacks because a stolen drive cannot be decrypted without the original machine's TPM. TPM 2.0 is required for Windows 11 and supports a wider range of cryptographic algorithms than TPM 1.2.

prompt: A technician installs a new Linux distribution and receives a boot error: 'Secure Boot violation — forbidden by firmware.' What is Secure Boot doing and what is the recommended way to proceed?

options.text: The Linux USB is corrupted — re-download the ISO
Secure Boot is rejecting an unsigned or untrusted bootloader — disable Secure Boot in UEFI settings or enroll the Linux bootloader key via MOK Manager
The hard drive is incompatible with Linux
The CPU does not support 64-bit operating systems

explanation: Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that checks the digital signature of every bootloader against a database of trusted keys before allowing it to execute. This prevents bootkits and rootkits from loading before the OS. Major Linux distributions such as Ubuntu, Fedora, and Debian ship with a Microsoft-signed shim bootloader and should work with Secure Boot enabled. Custom kernels, older distributions, or specialized builds may need: the Secure Boot option disabled in UEFI firmware settings (less secure), or enrollment of the signing key using MOK (Machine Owner Key) Manager via the mokutil utility in Linux. Disabling Secure Boot reduces protection against boot-level malware but does not affect normal OS operation.

prompt: A user visiting an internal company website sees: 'Your connection is not private — NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID.' What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The website is infected with malware
The website uses a TLS certificate signed by an internal CA that the browser does not trust by default
The user's internet connection is too slow for HTTPS
The website does not support modern encryption

explanation: This error means the Certificate Authority that signed the website's certificate is not in the browser's trust store. For internal or intranet sites, the likely causes are: an internal CA (the company operates its own certificate authority), a self-signed certificate (the server signed its own certificate with no CA vouching for it), an expired certificate, or a hostname mismatch. The fix is to distribute the company's root CA certificate to all devices via Group Policy (Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Public Key Policies → Trusted Root Certification Authorities). Once the internal CA is trusted, all certificates it issues are automatically trusted. Users should never click through this error on public websites; it may indicate a man-in-the-middle attack.

prompt: After a domain password change, a user receives repeated login prompts when accessing a mapped network drive. Where in Windows should the outdated cached credentials be updated?

options.text: Control Panel → User Accounts
Credential Manager → Windows Credentials — edit or remove the stale credential
Device Manager
Local Security Policy

explanation: Windows Credential Manager (Control Panel → User Accounts → Credential Manager) stores saved credentials for network resources, mapped drives, and domain resources under Windows Credentials, and browser-saved passwords under Web Credentials. After a password change, the old credential for the domain or server remains saved and causes repeated authentication failures. The fix is to open Credential Manager → Windows Credentials → find the entry for the affected server or domain → click Edit to update the password, or Remove to delete it (the next access will prompt for fresh credentials). Access via Run dialog: rundll32.exe keymgr.dll,KRShowKeyMgr. This is a common help desk task after password resets or domain password expirations.

prompt: A new business application needs to accept inbound TCP connections on port 8443 but is blocked on one specific workstation while working on others. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Disable Windows Defender Firewall entirely on the workstation
Open wf.msc and create a new inbound rule allowing TCP port 8443 for the appropriate network profiles
Uninstall Windows Defender Antivirus to remove the firewall blocking
Add the port to the HOSTS file

explanation: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security (wf.msc) provides granular rule control. To create an inbound rule: open wf.msc → Inbound Rules → New Rule → select Port → TCP → enter 8443 → Allow the connection → select the relevant profiles (Domain, Private, Public) → name the rule. For better security, rules can be scoped to a specific program executable rather than just a port number, limiting the rule to only that application. Group Policy can deploy firewall rules to all domain workstations centrally so the same configuration is enforced everywhere. Temporarily disabling the firewall to confirm it is the cause is an acceptable diagnostic step, but the firewall must be re-enabled immediately and the proper exception created.

prompt: An employee with a company-enrolled personal smartphone leaves the organization. IT needs to remove all corporate data without affecting the employee's personal photos and apps. Which MDM action accomplishes this?

options.text: Full factory reset — wipes everything including personal data
Selective (corporate) wipe — removes only MDM-managed corporate apps, email, and data while leaving personal content intact
Ask the employee to manually delete their work email app
Remote lock the device and leave all data in place

explanation: MDM selective wipe (also called corporate wipe or partial wipe) removes only the data and applications managed by the MDM solution: corporate email profiles and cached messages, MDM-pushed applications and their data, Wi-Fi and VPN configuration profiles, corporate certificates and access tokens. Personal content is not touched: photos, personal apps, personal contacts, text messages, music. Full factory reset is appropriate only for company-owned devices because it erases everything. Enrolling BYOD devices with a container approach (Android Work Profile or iOS Managed Apps) from the start ensures a clean separation between corporate and personal data, making selective wipe straightforward and legally defensible. Relying on employees to self-delete is not auditable or reliable.

prompt: A company policy requires all workstations to lock automatically after 5 minutes of inactivity, and users must not be able to change this setting. How is this enforced on domain-joined machines?

options.text: Each user configures their own screensaver in Settings
A Group Policy Object configures the screensaver timeout, enables password protection, and prevents users from changing the settings
Device Manager power settings control the lock timer
Windows Defender Security Center enforces the inactivity timeout

explanation: Group Policy enforces mandatory screen locking that users cannot override. The path is User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Control Panel → Personalization. Enable Screen Saver must be set to Enabled. Screen Saver timeout should be set to 300 seconds (5 minutes). Password protect the screen saver must be set to Enabled. Once these GPO settings are applied, the screensaver controls in the Settings app are grayed out and users cannot change them. An alternative approach using Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options → Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit directly locks the workstation session rather than using a screensaver, and also cannot be changed by the user.

prompt: A remote employee's VPN is configured so that traffic to corporate internal addresses (10.0.0.0/8) routes through the VPN tunnel, while general internet browsing goes directly to the ISP. What VPN configuration is this?

options.text: Full tunnel VPN — all traffic routes through the VPN
Split tunnel VPN — only corporate-bound traffic uses the VPN; internet traffic goes direct
Site-to-site VPN — connects office networks together
Reverse proxy — exposes internal resources to the internet

explanation: Split tunneling routes only traffic destined for specific corporate IP ranges through the encrypted VPN tunnel while all other internet traffic goes directly through the user's local ISP connection. Benefits: faster internet performance for users, conserves corporate bandwidth, reduces VPN gateway load. Drawbacks: corporate security controls (web filtering, DLP) do not apply to internet traffic; reduced visibility for the security team. Full tunnel routes ALL traffic through the VPN, including personal browsing. This gives maximum visibility and control but increases VPN gateway load and slows internet access. The choice between split and full tunnel is typically a policy decision made by IT and security teams and configured centrally, not by end users. Compliance-sensitive roles may require full tunnel to ensure all traffic is monitored.

prompt: A user hovers over a link in an email claiming to be from their bank. The status bar shows: http://1oginbank.suspicious-domain.xyz. What are the red flags?

options.text: The email is legitimate — banks frequently send verification links
The domain does not match the bank's real domain, the link uses HTTP not HTTPS, and '1ogin' uses the digit 1 instead of the letter l — all classic phishing indicators
Only the HTTP protocol is suspicious; the rest is acceptable
The professional appearance of the email confirms it is legitimate

explanation: Multiple phishing red flags are present: Domain mismatch: suspicious-domain.xyz is not the bank's registered domain. Homograph substitution: using the digit 1 in place of lowercase l in '1ogin' creates a visually similar but different URL — a common phishing trick. Unencrypted HTTP: legitimate banking sites always use HTTPS. Additional indicators to look for: urgent language ('your account will be locked in 24 hours'), generic greeting ('Dear Customer' instead of your name), unexpected email from the institution, and requests for credentials or personal information. The safest response is always to navigate directly to the bank's website by typing the known URL, rather than clicking any email link. Users should report suspected phishing emails to the IT or security team.

prompt: A financial firm requires MFA that cannot be defeated by real-time phishing proxy attacks. Which MFA method is MOST resistant to this threat?

options.text: SMS one-time codes sent to a registered phone number
Email-based OTP codes
FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security key bound cryptographically to the registered website origin
TOTP authenticator app generating 6-digit codes

explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security keys (such as YubiKey or Google Titan) are the most phishing-resistant MFA available.
